title: Sample spaces & two-way tables
examples: Can you show me how to fill in the missing numbers in this table?
If I roll two dice, what is the total number of possible outcomes?
How do I use a diagram to list all the possibilities?

explain.say: Today we look at sample spaces and tables. We find all possible outcomes together. Consider flipping one coin twice. The possible results are heads heads, heads tails, tails heads, and tails tails.

draw.text: Coin flips: HH, HT, TH, TT

explain.say: We can use a diagram to list these outcomes. We list one result on the top and another on the side. This helps us see every single combination clearly.
Next we look at two-way tables. These tables help us organize data from two different groups. For example, we can see preferences for two different colours.
We fill the table by counting how many times each combination happens. If we have ten people, we count how many like blue and how many like red. This organizes our findings.

faq.q: What is a sample space exactly?
faq.a: A sample space is simply the set of all possible results of an experiment. For example, rolling a standard die means the sample space is one, two, three, four, five, and six.
asks: What are all the possible outcomes?
List all the possibilities for me.

faq.q: Do I always have to use a diagram?
faq.a: No, sometimes a simple list works fine for small problems. However, a diagram or table helps keep you organized and prevents you from missing any outcomes.

faq.q: How do I read the totals in a two-way table?
faq.a: The totals tell you the overall count for a row or a column. You add up the numbers across a row or down a column to find that total.
asks: How do I find the grand total?

faq.q: Can I use this for probability too?
faq.a: Yes, absolutely. Once you have the table, you can find the probability by counting the favourable outcomes over the total number of outcomes.

faq.q: If I flip two coins, is the order important?
faq.a: Yes, the order is very important. Heads then tails is a different outcome from tails then heads. We treat them as separate results.
asks: Does HT count the same as TH?
Does order matter for coin flips?

facts: A sample space lists every single possible outcome of an event.
A two-way table organizes data based on two different characteristics.
The total number of outcomes is found by multiplying the number of options in each category.
Probability is calculated as favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.

quiz.say: When tossing two coins, what is the complete sample space?
quiz.why: There are four unique outcomes when flipping two coins, so the space includes all four combinations.

wrong.0: You missed one of the possible combinations in the set.
wrong.1: Mixing single results with pairs makes the list confusing.
wrong.3: This only lists the two different results, ignoring the order.

quiz.say: In a table of 20 students, 12 like apples and 10 like bananas. How many like both?
quiz.why: You use the formula to find the overlap, ensuring you do not count anyone twice.

wrong.0: Adding the two groups together counts the overlapping people twice.
wrong.1: This only gives you the count for one of the groups.
wrong.2: This is the total, not the number who like both things.

quiz.say: If a table has 3 rows and 4 columns, what is the total number of outcomes?
quiz.why: You multiply the number of options in the rows by the number of options in the columns.

wrong.0: This is adding the number of rows and the number of columns together.
wrong.1: This suggests there is only one total outcome possible.
wrong.2: You incorrectly calculated the product of three and four.
